Slack
slak
adj. and v. (loose, remiss, slow; to delay or let go)
Saxon slac, loose or remiss. The word runs through Scripture as the opposite of diligence and, in Peter's hands, becomes the answer to the oldest objection against the second coming.

Biblical Definition

“The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance” (2Pe 3:9). The scoffers had asked where the promise of His coming was, since all things continue as they were; Peter answers that the delay is not remissness but patience, and that the interval is mercy — time given for repentance. Read in its context the verse is not about God wishing to save every individual without exception while failing to do so; Peter is writing to the beloved, and the any and all are the us-ward he has just named, the elect for whose ingathering the world is still standing. The rest of the word's uses set the human standard. Vows: “thou shalt not slack to pay it: for the LORD thy God will surely require it of thee” (Deu 23:21). Labour: “He becometh poor that dealeth with a slack hand: but the hand of the diligent maketh rich” (Pro 10:4). Warfare: Gibeon's cry, “Slack not thy hand from thy servants; come up to us quickly” (Jos 10:6). Conquest: “How long are ye slack to go to possess the land, which the LORD God of your fathers hath given you?” (Jos 18:3). And judgment: He “will not be slack to him that hateth him” (Deu 7:10).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines slack as not tense, loose; remiss, backward, not diligent; and slow, not quick or prompt.

expand to see more

SLACK, a. Not tense; not hard drawn; not firmly extended; as a slack rope.

1. Weak; remiss; not holding fast; as a slack hand.

2. Slow; not prompt; tardy; as, to be slack in duty.

3. Not violent; not rapid; as a slack pace.

SLACKNESS, n. Remissness; negligence; inattention; want of eagerness.

Key Scripture

2Pe 3:9 — "The Lord is not slack concerning his promise, as some men count slackness; but is longsuffering to us-ward, not willing that any should perish, but that all should come to repentance."

Jos 18:3 — "And Joshua said unto the children of Israel, How long are ye slack to go to possess the land, which the LORD God of your fathers hath given you?"

Deu 23:21 — "When thou shalt vow a vow unto the LORD thy God, thou shalt not slack to pay it: for the LORD thy God will surely require it of thee; and it would be sin in thee."

Pro 10:4 — "He becometh poor that dealeth with a slack hand: but the hand of the diligent maketh rich."

Modern Corruption

God's patience is read as indifference or as universal salvation; Peter calls it longsuffering with an end in view.

expand to see more

Two opposite errors are built on 2 Peter 3:9. The scoffers Peter names draw one: the delay proves nothing is coming, since all things continue as they were from the beginning. Peter answers with the flood — the world that then was, being overflowed with water, perished — and with the fire reserved for this one. The other error reads not willing that any should perish as a universal saving intention that fails, which would make God's purpose defeatable by the creature. Peter is writing to the beloved and speaks of longsuffering to us-ward; the delay is the gathering of the elect, and every day of it is mercy toward people not yet born.

The human side of the word deserves the sharper application. Joshua 18:3 was addressed to seven tribes who had won the land and had not gone in to take their portions — possessing what God had already given proved harder than fighting for it. That is a familiar shape. Believers who would face persecution bravely can spend years slack toward the promises actually held out to them: the mortification of a known sin, the family worship never begun, the vow made and not paid. Thou shalt not slack to pay it is written to such men.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew 'achar (H309), to delay, to be slack; raphah (H7503), to sink, relax, let drop; Greek braduno (G1019), to be slow or tardy.

expand to see more

Hebrew 'achar (H309) — to delay, to tarry; Deuteronomy 23:21, thou shalt not slack to pay thy vow.

Hebrew raphah (H7503) — to sink down, to relax, to let go; Joshua 10:6 (slack not thy hand), Zephaniah 3:16.

Hebrew remiyyah (H7423) — slackness, deceit, negligence; Proverbs 10:4, a slack hand — the same word rendered deceitful elsewhere.

Greek braduno (G1019) — to be slow, to delay; 2 Peter 3:9, 1 Timothy 3:15.

Greek makrothumeo (G3114) — to be longsuffering, patient of spirit; the word Peter sets against slackness.

Usage

"“The Lord is not slack… but is longsuffering” — the delay is the mercy."

"“How long are ye slack to go to possess the land” — seven tribes, already victorious."

"“He becometh poor that dealeth with a slack hand”."
